draft.title: Multiplying and dividing powers
card: A power has a base and an index. In 3⁴, the base is 3 and the index is 4, so 3⁴ = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3.
Multiply
when the bases are the same, add the indices. 3⁴ × 3² = 3⁽⁴⁺²⁾ = 3⁶. This works because 3⁴ has four 3s and 3² has two more, so there are six 3s in all.
Divide
when the bases are the same, subtract the indices. 5⁷ ÷ 5³ = 5⁽⁷⁻³⁾ = 5⁴. Three of the seven 5s cancel with the three 5s below.
Only the indices are added or subtracted. The base stays the same. These rules need the same base, so they do not apply to 2⁴ × 3² as it stands.
draft.remember: Same base: add the indices to multiply, subtract them to divide, and keep the base.

a.q: Which is 7⁵ × 7³ written as a single power?
a.why: Multiplying powers with the same base adds the indices: 5 + 3 = 8, so the answer is 7⁸. 7¹⁵ is tempting, but it comes from multiplying the indices, which is not the rule here.
a.clue: The base stays the same. What do you do to the indices?

b.q: Which is 6⁹ ÷ 6⁴ × 6² written as a single power?
b.why: Work from left to right: 6⁹ ÷ 6⁴ = 6⁵, then 6⁵ × 6² = 6⁷. Check: 9 − 4 + 2 = 7. 6³ comes from subtracting both 4 and 2 instead of adding the 2.
b.clue: Divide means subtract the indices. Multiply means add them.

problems.detail: The card never shows dividing and multiplying in one expression, or the left-to-right rule for ÷ and ×. Some students may read 6⁹ ÷ 6⁴ × 6² as 6⁹ ÷ (6⁴ × 6²) and pick 6³. The why relies on 'work from left to right', which the card does not teach.

check.summary: The card and question a are correct. Question b mixes ÷ and × and depends on the left-to-right order of operations, which the card does not teach. Consider adding a mixed example to the card or rewording the question.

final.title: Multiplying and dividing powers
card: A power has a base and an index. In \(3^{4}\), the base is 3 and the index is 4, so \(3^{4} = 3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3\).
Multiply
when the bases are the same, add the indices. \(3^{4} \times 3^{2} = 3^{4 + 2} = 3^{6}\). This works because \(3^{4}\) has four 3s and \(3^{2}\) has two more, so there are six 3s in all.
Divide
when the bases are the same, subtract the indices. \(5^{7} \div 5^{3} = 5^{7 - 3} = 5^{4}\). Three of the seven 5s cancel with the three 5s below.
Only the indices change. The base stays the same. The rules need the same base, so they do not apply to \(2^{4} \times 3^{2}\) as it stands. If there are brackets, work them out first.
final.remember: Same base: add the indices to multiply, subtract them to divide, and keep the base.

a.q: Which is \(7^{5} \times 7^{3}\) written as a single power?
a.why: Multiplying powers with the same base adds the indices: \(5 + 3 = 8\), so the answer is \(7^{8}\). \(7^{15}\) is tempting, but it comes from multiplying the indices, which is not the rule here.
a.clue: The base stays the same. What do you do to the indices?

b.q: Which is \((2^{5} \times 2^{6}) \div 2^{3}\) written as a single power?
b.why: Do the brackets first: \(2^{5} \times 2^{6} = 2^{11}\). Then \(2^{11} \div 2^{3} = 2^{8}\), as \(11 - 3 = 8\). \(2^{14}\) is tempting, but it comes from adding the 3 when dividing means subtracting it.
b.clue: Multiply means add the indices. Divide means subtract them.
